body.text: On Sunday, a third straight day of talks was held in Doha between Iranian negotiators and Qatari mediators. Afterward, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the plan’s timeline for reopening the Strait of Hormuz had been shortened from seven days to two. Sanctions relief, a reduced U.S. military presence, and recognition of new shipping routes designated by Iran and Oman are among the conditions put forward. Tehran presented these demands as its response to months of war and the U.S. blockade of its ports, while Washington warned it will consider other options if normal navigation is not restored.
Two days earlier, however, a ship that had been cleared for passage was struck. Safe transit is not guaranteed even with Iran’s permission.

The ship was carrying gas bound for Pakistan, and its clearance had been arranged by Islamabad. According to people familiar with the shipment who spoke to Bloomberg, safe passage for the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda had been negotiated by Pakistan before the vessel was struck near the strait on October 30. Until then, it had seemed that Pakistan’s diplomacy was producing concrete results: Several earlier cargoes cleared the same way had crossed safely.

With renewed strikes being weighed in Washington after the November 3 midterms and a forceful response promised by Tehran, the incident leads to a clear conclusion: Pakistan can broker access, but it has little recourse if those commitments are later ignored.

Pakistan’s mediation record this year is substantial. Islamabad hosted the talks that produced the interim memorandum reached in June, and Field Marshal Asim Munir traveled to Tehran twice in October, after which a Pakistani military spokesman called Islamabad “cautiously optimistic” while warning of “powerful spoilers and detractors.” Qatar, which is hosting the current round of talks, is actively partnering with Pakistan in these efforts.

Such achievements are made possible by Pakistan’s ability to talk to both sides while threatening neither. But the Hormuz crisis increasingly demands a guarantor – and this is a role Pakistan is ill-equipped to fill. The Al Mayeda case illustrates the problem. The vessel’s passage was cleared through Pakistan’s good offices, but the promise was swiftly broken – and Islamabad could do nothing about it.

Responsibility for the attack has not been established, and no one has claimed it. Qatar is investigating the attack. The Strait of Hormuz has become a contested space in which a number of actors carried out a record number of strikes in October. Tehran has submitted evidence to the International Maritime Organization of alleged U.S. and Israeli attacks on its own ports and vessels. In such an environment, a ship cleared through Pakistan’s channel becomes an obvious target for those who would rather see the talks fail, consistent with the warning about “spoilers” issued by Pakistan’s military spokesman. Regardless of who was responsible, the strike damaged the credibility on which Pakistan’s mediation rests.

Pakistan’s energy exposure compounds the problem. Imported LNG – nearly all of traversing Hormuz – met about a fifth of its gas demand last year, yet Pakistan received just two Qatari cargoes in October against eight a year earlier. QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure to December 29, and spot cargoes cost roughly double the contract price. Islamabad’s engagement with Tehran on safe passage is a product of close neighborly relations, but it also ties Pakistan’s energy security to the fate of the talks. The longer Hormuz remains insecure, the higher the economic cost of Pakistan’s mediation role.

In keeping with Pakistan’s consistent preference for dialogue over force, the answer is not to step back from mediation but to share the burden of guaranteeing compliance. The June memorandum was facilitated alongside Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, Qatar, and Egypt, and Qatar now leads the Doha track. A multilateral deconfliction arrangement for neutral energy cargoes would spread the reputational risk and raise the diplomatic cost for anyone who puts a cleared ship at risk. A collective assurance is far harder to ignore than a Pakistani one.

Islamabad also needs to separate its energy security from its mediator role. Pakistan is reportedly considering buying ten spot cargoes worth more than $1 billion and sourcing supplies from the United States and Azerbaijan. Such diversification is expensive, but doing nothing may cost more in the long run. Energy security is not merely sound economic policy but a precondition for credible mediation.

Just as important, Pakistan should be candid with all parties about what it can deliver. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has confirmed that talks are ongoing but offered no timeframe, and President Donald Trump says he is in no rush. Islamabad can pass messages, host talks, and test proposals, but it cannot verify any party’s conduct at sea. If Pakistan exaggerates its role, it would become the obvious scapegoat if a plan to reopen Hormuz collapses. With the fate of negotiations uncertain, Islamabad’s credibility is best protected by claiming less.

Middle power mediation has gained prominence this year, with Qatar, Turkiye, Oman, and Pakistan all finding new relevance as great power crises multiply. Yet the events of 2026 have exposed the limits of that role: mediators can reduce the cost of negotiating, but they cannot guarantee compliance once an agreement is reached. As debate continues in Doha over how ships will pass safely through the Strait of Hormuz, the strike on the Al Mayeda reminds us that promises alone cannot protect vessels.
